props.title: Goodbye to Language

sections.content: Jean-Luc Godard's **Goodbye to Language (2014)** (2014) represents a radical experiment in 3D filmmaking that shatters conventional narrative. Like his groundbreaking **Breathless** (1960), Godard deliberately fractures cinematic grammar, but now weaponizes stereoscopic technology. The film splits 3D images apart, forcing each eye to see different scenes - a technical innovation that makes Hollywood's 3D look primitive. It's part of Godard's late-career abstract phase, following Film Socialisme (2010) and **Notre Musique** (2004), where he pushes cinema's boundaries through digital manipulation.

movies.title: Adieu au langage
movies.slug: Experimental 3D film about a couple and a dog, fracturing narrative and visual space

sections.content: The film's radical approach to 3D connects to a broader movement of experimental stereoscopic work. **Pina** (2011) used 3D to capture dance in revolutionary ways, while **Cave of Forgotten Dreams** (2010) employed it to explore ancient art. But Godard goes further, literally breaking the technology's rules. He forces viewers to choose which eye to follow during key sequences, creating a physically demanding viewing experience that questions how we process images.

Like fellow avant-garde pioneer **Hollis Frampton** with **Zorns Lemma** (1970), Godard strips cinema down to its basic elements - light, sound, movement - then rebuilds it in radical new configurations. The film's dog, Roxy, becomes a lens through which to view human behavior, recalling the animal perspectives in **Heart of a Dog** (2015) and **Le Quattro Volte** (2010). SUBHEAD: Digital Experimentation and Modern Cinema

Godard's digital manipulations connect to contemporary experimental filmmakers like **Peter Greenaway** with **The Pillow Book** (1996) and **Prospero's Books** (1991). The layered images, text overlays, and deliberate video artifacts create a dense visual language that comments on modern media saturation. This approach influenced later works like **The Congress** (2013) and **Creative Control** (2015).
